criteria.note: The core answer to "gluten in korean food" — that the risk sits in fermented condiments rather than the visible dish — lands roughly 60 words in, well inside the first 200 words, and the condiment table follows immediately.

Title is 35 chars (55 with the rendered ' | Gluten-Free Korea' suffix), description is ~148 chars, the keyword appears in both, and the description adds three distinct hooks rather than restating the title.

Headings carry the argument rather than label sections — a skimmer moving from "The fermented condiment problem" to "The allergen line only covers wheat" to "The 'rice bread' trap" to "control the condiments, reclaim the cuisine" gets the full thesis.

Three distinct internal destinations, each placed where the reader would actually want them: the label guide at the allergen-line gap, the restaurant list at the eating-out step, and the pillar guide as the entry point.

All three FAQ answers are traceable to body claims (Sempio 501 wheat listing, fish cake wheat starch, dangmyeon sweet potato starch plus mixed-starch caveat) and each reads as a complete standalone answer in a rich result.

Named specifics and things that went wrong: a named anchor restaurant closing for remodel, a loaf whose "gluten-free" label was quietly renamed a week later, a named Yeonnam shop selling travel packets, and named chains stocking tamari.

Consistent hangul-plus-romanisation throughout, a specific product line (Sempio 양조간장 501), the specific regulatory instrument (식품등의 표시기준 별표 2), and the three distinct label routes wheat takes into gochujang — all checkable by a reader holding a package.

The two load-bearing claims are anchored to primary sources — the manufacturer's own product page and the MFDS labeling standard — each with a retrieval date and a note that the standard is amended regularly.
An explicit scope-and-limits paragraph states what label-reading cannot establish, the Goraesa lead is flagged as unverified, and there are no affiliate or commercial links requiring disclosure.

findings.quote: **Soy sauce → imported Japanese tamari.** The easiest wheat-free substitute to find in Seoul
findings.why: The article's strongest practical section — the actual replacement condiments — drops to category level exactly where a reader most needs a product name, while the rest of the piece names things precisely (Sempio 양조간장 501, monil2 house). A reader in a Lotte Mart aisle cannot act on "imported Japanese tamari" the way they can act on the rest of the guide.
findings.fix: Name the specific tamari brand and the specific gluten-free gochujang currently in the kitchen, with the 원재료명 line that clears each, and add a retrieved-date so a later reformulation is visible as such.

findings.quote: We have not found a Korean equivalent of [GFCO](https://gfco.org)
findings.why: This is a negative claim about the whole Korean certification landscape, and it carries real weight in the argument that a front-of-package claim is unaudited here. The GFCO link documents what GFCO is, not that no Korean counterpart exists, so the sentence rests on absence of evidence with no method attached.
findings.fix: State how the absence was checked and when — for example which MFDS certification registries or industry association lists were searched, with a retrieval date — or soften to a scoped claim about what the MFDS standard does and does not require of a voluntary gluten-free claim.

criteria.note: Load-bearing claims are anchored to manufacturer and regulatory sources or explicitly marked as the authors' own observation; one concrete third-party product claim is asserted without source or link.
criteria.evidence_quote: in Yeonnam sells travel-sized packets of gluten-free gochujang and soy sauce

criteria.note: Product names (Sempio 양조간장 501, 고래사, 237 Pizza, GFCO) are real and checkable, no statistics are asserted, and the July date plus the August update note are internally consistent.
The piece states exactly how it knows what it knows and names three things the method cannot establish — brand-level coverage, reformulation, and trace gluten from shared equipment.

Cross-contamination is addressed repeatedly and celiac risk is correctly escalated above NCGS, but one categorical composition claim about 떡 is stated without the caveat given to the comparable dangmyeon case.
criteria.evidence_quote: 떡 (*tteok*, rice cake) itself is gluten-free.

criteria.note: Both external sources carry August 2026 retrieval dates, the MFDS standard is flagged as amended regularly, and manufacturer reformulation is named as a live risk.
The mandatory-allergen scope is stated correctly — wheat declared, barley and rye not — and the Korean terms, romanizations and 밀쌀/소맥분 distinctions are right.
The reader gets the exact Korean strings to scan, a direct link to the manufacturer page and the MFDS standard, and a linked four-step label method rather than being asked to trust the piece.

findings.quote: 떡 (*tteok*, rice cake) itself is gluten-free.
findings.why: 밀떡 — tteokbokki rice cake made with wheat flour — is a mainstream Korean product sold in supermarkets and used at street stalls, so 떡 is not a category that can be cleared wholesale. The article gives dangmyeon an explicit mixed-starch warning but gives 떡 none, and it recommends the home version of tteokbokki as the safe path, which sends a celiac reader to buy tteok under a categorical assurance. A reader acting reasonably on this sentence can buy 밀떡 and eat wheat.
findings.fix: Qualify both instances the way dangmyeon is qualified: state that 떡 made from rice is gluten-free but that 밀떡 (wheat-flour rice cake) is common in tteokbokki, and that the 원재료명 must be checked for 밀/소맥분 on any tteok bought for home cooking.

findings.quote: in Yeonnam sells travel-sized packets of gluten-free gochujang and soy sauce
findings.why: This is a concrete third-party claim that a named business sells gluten-free versions of the two condiments the article has just identified as the biggest hidden-gluten source. It carries no link, no product name, no retrieval date, and no marker that it is the authors' own observation — and it is exactly the kind of front-of-package gluten-free claim the article elsewhere teaches readers to distrust. A reader will act on it.
findings.fix: Either link the shop and name the specific products with a retrieval date, or mark it as an unverified first-hand observation and repeat the article's own standing rule — that a gluten-free claim on the packet is where checking starts, not where it finishes, and that the 원재료명 still has to be read.
